message.content:
Let  
\[
S=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\cos(n\theta)}{2^n}.
\]
Using Euler’s formula,
\[
S=\Re\left(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}\right)^n\right).
\]
Since \(\left|\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}\right|=\frac12<1\), the geometric series converges:
\[
\sum_{n=0}^\infty \left(\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}\right)^n
=\frac{1}{1-\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}}.
\]
Thus
\[
S=\Re\left(\frac{1}{1-\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}}\right).
\]
Compute the real part:
\[
\frac{1}{1-\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}}
=\frac{1-\frac{e^{-i\theta}}{2}}{\left|1-\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}\right|^2}.
\]
The denominator is
\[
\left|1-\frac{e^{i\theta}}{2}\right|^2
=1-\cos\theta+\frac14
=\frac54-\cos\theta.
\]
The numerator’s real part is
\[
1-\frac{\cos\theta}{2}.
\]
Given \(\cos\theta=\frac15\),
\[
S=\frac{1-\frac{1}{10}}{\frac54-\frac15}
=\frac{\frac{9}{10}}{\frac{21}{20}}
=\frac{9}{10}\cdot\frac{20}{21}
=\frac{6}{7}.
\]

The answer is \(\boxed{\frac{6}{7}}\).
